metadata.title: What is Godot?
metadata.note: Narrated by Yeshwanth on the @HumanitariansAI channel — NOT a claude-liam reel, so OUTRO-LOCK's @NikBearBrown card is deliberately not used (see BUILD-LOG.md). Reel-local components live in the toolkit at runtime/remotion/src/GodotReadable.tsx; the renderer can only see components inside its own project.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Yeshwanth, and this video is about what Godot is and why it's a great fit for building games with AI. Not long ago, making a game meant months of writing code by hand, line after line. That's changing, and it's changing fast. Let me show you the tool that's a big part of why.

the question types itself into the composer
send button arms terracotta; running indicator appears
three output lines land one at a time — the answer arrives before the story starts

props.command: What is Godot, and why is it the right engine for building a game with AI?
output: A free, open-source engine for 2D and 3D games.
It saves everything as plain text — scenes, settings, scripts.
So an AI can read your whole project, and change it safely.

beats.act: the whole idea in one breath (BLUF)
beats.narration_text: So here's the whole idea in one breath, before any of the details. Godot is a tool for anyone with an idea, not just for programmers. It's free. It makes both 2D and 3D games. And it saves everything it makes as plain text. That last part sounds small, but it is the one that matters, because it is the reason an AI like Claude can do most of the building while you sit and direct it. Everything else in this video is really just an explanation of that one sentence.

it deletes back and types 'anyone with an idea' — the misconception this video exists to fix

props.text:
Godot is a tool for programmers.
It is free.
It makes 2D and 3D games.
It saves what it makes
as plain text.
That is why an AI
can build in it with you.

beats.narration_text: So what is it, exactly? Godot is a free, open-source tool for making games. Free with no catch — there's no licence to buy, and no fee later if your game makes money. It handles flat 2D games, like a side-scroller or a puzzle, and it handles full 3D worlds you can walk around inside. One download, both kinds.

show.event: chip 'Free forever — no licence' lands, terracotta, the one accent
chip 'No fee if your game sells' lands
chip '2D — platformers, puzzles' lands
chip '3D — worlds you walk in' lands; caption settles beneath the grid

items.label: No fee if your game sells

props.caption: One download. Open source. Nothing to buy, ever.

beats.narration_text: Now, how you actually build something in it. A Godot game is made of small pieces called nodes, and you snap them together a bit like LEGO bricks. One node is your character. Another is the picture you see on screen. Another plays a sound. You arrange a handful of them into what's called a scene, and that scene becomes your player, or your level. There's no wall of code to get started.

shot.new_visual_element: Node tree in plain language, with the attached script

show.event: the parent node 'Player' draws in at the top of the tree
child nodes branch down in narration order: the picture, the hitbox, the sound
each node's plain-language note lights as the voice names what it does
the script card slides in beside the tree, showing what attaches behaviour
tree and script hold side by side

beats.narration_text: When you want something to actually move, you add a short script. The language is called GDScript, and it reads almost like plain English — it's very close to Python, if you've ever met that. Here's a real one. Read it slowly with me: if the player presses right, move right. If they press left, move left. Otherwise, stand still. That's the whole file, and that is genuinely how it reads.

show.event: file tab reads 'player.gd', language chip reads GDSCRIPT
lines stagger in one at a time, matching the pace the voice reads them
both input lines are on screen together as the voice says 'press right / press left'
the whole file sits on screen at once — short enough to read in one look

props.title: player.gd

beats.act: the heart — why this matters for AI
beats.narration_text: And here is the part that matters most, the reason we're talking about Godot at all. Godot saves everything you make as plain text — the kind you could open in any notepad. Your scenes, your settings, your scripts, all of it. So an AI can open your project, actually read it, change it safely, and then show you exactly what changed, line by line. Other big engines seal their work inside a format only that engine can open. An AI can't safely touch that. This is the reason Godot is the fit.

shot.new_visual_element: Sealed file vs plain text: the same change made to both

show.event: two panels open side by side — left 'Other engines · sealed file', right 'Godot · plain text'

the same change is made to both — left shows 'something changed, you cannot see what'
right shows it as a plain before-and-after, the new line in terracotta
'you see exactly what changed' settles under the right panel

props.sparkLine: One of them you can read.
props.leftNote: Only the engine can open it

beats.narration_text: And that is exactly what we do here. We take an old game, hand its logic over to Claude Code, and have it rebuild that game in Godot — by conversation. You describe what you want. It builds it. You play it, tell it what felt wrong, and it changes it. You are directing the work, not typing it out.

show.event: composer returns — here the interface IS the subject, because it is the workflow
the rebuild instruction types itself in
running indicator reads 'rebuilding in Godot…'
output lines land as the loop the voice describes: describe, build, play, refine

props.segment: Describe it, play it, refine it
props.command: Here is the old game's logic. Rebuild it in Godot — make the player move, then let me play it and tell you what to change.
output: Reading the logic → writing the scenes and the scripts.
You play it. You say what felt wrong.
It changes the files, and you watch every change happen.

beats.narration_text: So if you have been waiting until you learn to code — you don't need to be a programmer to start. You need an idea, and a tool that lets an AI do the heavy lifting. Godot: free, readable, and built for making games with AI.
